newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU gene label decision seen in need of follow-up.
newsitem.headline: EU gene label decision seen in need of follow-up.

text.p: Last week's European Commission move to include genetically modified soya and maize in the EU novel food law is a positive step but the law is not yet workable, German food industry institute BLL said.
"The EU move is the right way to offer comprehensive information on the use of biotechnology in food products," said BLL's scientific adviser Christiane Toussaint.

"But the EU only has until November 1 to decide what goes on food labels, by what time industries across the EU will have to comply and what transition periods will be allowed for food products already in the distribution chain."

Toussaint said BLL had been pressing for faster decisions for many months and was concerned industries in the 15-nation bloc had no harmonised implementation guidelines to comply with the novel food law, which came into force on May 15.
The directive requires labelling for bio-engineered food which differs from conventional foods beyond accepted limits of natural variation.
Genetically modified soya and maize had so far escaped the rule because they were introduced in the EU before the novel food law.
The EU move was aimed at closing this legislative gap.

BLL, which supplies scientific and legal services to 300 food producers and traders, said the EU needed to draw up a list of the products that needed labelling, how they would have to be labelled, and how this should be monitored.

"The process won't be made easier by disagreement in the EU over what is necessary, there appears to be a consensus in Germany and the Netherlands, but Britain's stance is completely different from that," Toussaint said.
"As long as there is no clarity, companies operating in more than one country are left guessing how to operate and consumers will be confused."

A spokesman for the German operations of multi-national food group Unilever said the EU move was positive for consumers and the company would fully comply with any labelling demands made by legislators.
It expected labelling rules would apply to soya protein.
